review_text_raw:
I cautiously recommend this game. It's great on the whole, but there were a couple design choices which [b]really[/b] bugged me and nearly caused me to give a thumbs down. Those two things were: [b]the usage of RNG & the game's subsequent reliance on rollbacks (do-overs).[/b]

I'm a huge fan of hacking games. They are one of my favorite niche-genres of games. Generally speaking, the gameplay in a hacking game follows a simple formula: poke at a "server" and strip its defenses using various tools until it can be "connected to." This is often done with a time limit.

Midnight Protocol challenges this formula by translating the process into a turn based affair. In many ways, it plays like a turn based RPG. On a conceptual level, this is a cool idea. I was excited when I read about it. In practice, however, I found that it [strike]encouraged[/strike] [b]mandated[/b] save scumming. I mean this as constructively as possible - [b]I hate this.[/b]

I'll elaborate:

When I was forced to repeat a mission in [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b], it was because I wasn't fast enough. The onus was on [b]ME[/b] to improve my skills. I needed to be faster. I had all the tools, but I came up short.

When I was forced to repeat a mission in [b][i]Midnight Protocol[/i][/b], it was because [b]the game's RNG[/b] dealt me an [i]objectively unwinnable[/i] scenario. The SysOp wandered into my node, or the "random" trace mechanic in Pavo's mission installed a Sundrop 10 nodes away.

This isn't interesting or engaging gameplay. I'm not learning anything, and I'm not becoming a better player. I'm just waiting for a luckier break.

Now, it would be one thing if you could "embrace failure" like you can in a game like XCOM or Rimworld - but you can't in Midnight Protocol. Most key missions actually prevent you from disconnecting until you complete your main objective. You are expected to rollback if you fail.

[i]My next two particular criticisms were addressed in a patch on 10/18/21. Respect.[/i]

[strike]RNG isn't the only thing causing me to rollback missions. The game gives you a peek at what kind of nodes & defenses you will be up against, allowing you to choose the appropriate programs for the job. For rank & file side-missions, this generally isn't a big deal. But for some of the larger story missions, you need fairly specific loadouts to have a fighting chance. It's not uncommon for me to get 8+ turns into a mission before I find myself thinking "Yeah I can't do this without Tunnel" and rolling back.

But it gets a little worse - ICE can be hidden... [i]and its location in missions is static.[/i] This means that after I (am forced to) rollback, I now know where the ICE is, and the mission is partially spoiled. It's up to me if I want to "pretend" not to know that.[/strike]

I've spent a lot of real estate here ragging on the RNG/Rollback mechanics, but I want to reiterate that I still recommend this game.

When the RNG gods [i]aren't[/i] busy strangling me, I actually really enjoy the turn based gameplay. It's a welcome twist on the genre that makes it feel truly different. The presentation is phenomenal (would have liked some more lively music though). And I really like the open ended narrative allowing you to chase leads & reply to emails. Simulation is an important part of hacking games, and I love the agency that the game gives us.

Well polished hacking games are an extreme rarity. There's been like... 5 since Uplink came out in 2001. I'm happy this game exists and I'm enjoying my time with it on the whole. I just wish RNG wasn't so strongly relied upon in its design.

review_text_raw:
[b]My Playtime:[/b] 29h (100% achievement, finished the game)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (~9 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] is a simple turn-based strategy game with a hacking theme. You'll be able to explore nodes in a network and use programs to get data from them. The game offers multiple story branching, missions, and unlockables based on the path that you choose.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- Story branching depends on your choice in the mission
- 2 endings
- Those who don't like to read can still enjoy the game without doing so
- Various programs and hardware to use based on the mission and playstyle
- Difficulty can be changed anytime you want

[b]Cons:[/b]
- RNG-based, especially at the beginning of the game
- It can take a while to wait until the enemy finishes their turn
- Missions will be treated as finished if you exit the network
- Contrasting colors in some cutscenes (red on top of black/grey) can be problematic to some people

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you enjoy playing hacking games and don't mind playing one in a different genre, buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The visuals are divided into two parts: your computer and the network interface. The computer interface is more simplified, giving a lot of space to the text with switchable tabs. As for the network, they are depicted with a lot of interconnected nodes that you can travel to. To be honest, they don't look like a network at all, but the programs' visuals help to give that impression.

[h3]Story[/h3]
Dialogues in [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] are mostly about missions that you will take. A lot of events will happen at the same time as the main plot, which will get you involved in various things. I liked that they usually don't stop after one mission - it feels as if I was involved and making progress. As for the main plot, I found them to be alright. The presentation looks cool with the sudden contract of color, although some parts are still in mystery. The closure also feels realistic with everything going by as normal. However, despite the multiple endings, I don't think they differ that much to warrant another playthrough.

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
As I said before, the game is a turn-based strategy, albeit simplified. You'll have a series of interconnected nodes where you can travel and spawn programs to help you with your objectives. The objectives are varied in each mission, but basically, you need to explore all nodes and take out every object of interest, whether it's by downloading a file or routing money to your account. Some ICEs will guard some nodes in between, forcing you to spawn another program to take them out. Moreover, you need to do these while avoiding being traced, which will be randomized per turn based on your stealth capabilities.

Stealth is the most problematic aspect of this game. You only have a 75% chance not to be recognized enemy for each turn, and that's by using all of your slices, which is the equivalent of your system memory in-game. However, you will eventually need to summon more programs to do other things, which will require more slices. You can always lower the assigned slices in your stealth program, but doing so will lower its capabilities, making it easier for you to be traced by the enemy. I had to restart a mission several times in the beginning whenever the RNG screw me up and traced me every turn. It was boring to replay the missions and do the same thing again, hoping that the outcome will be different. The gear upgrades that were given after you play some missions help to overcome this, but you still need to tough it out before you got to that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759479057

The early game is tough. Not only is the stealth mechanic isn't reliable, but the randomized enemies also can screw your run. You need to walk efficiently and not waste turns due to the RNG-based stealth, but enemies' locations are always hidden until you ran into them or used a sniffer program. Both options are not good either - the first option will increase your trace bar while the second one will eat 2 slices for 2 turns. It is easier to memorize enemies' locations before attempting your real run, but some enemies are placed randomly between more than one path. Again, this can be mitigated by purchasing upgrades after you reach a certain point.

The game gets better after you get enough upgrades. The RNG-based gameplay is still there, but it won't affect much to your experience. Moreover, numerous programs are available to help you build a deck that suits your playstyle. Since some missions are easier if you bring a certain program, you're bound to swap the programs from time to time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2632524112

The reputation system can increase your difficulty. The game has a system that categorizes you into either white hat, grey hat, or black hat. This gives an impression that you can only choose one, although you can get as many reputations as you want in all categories. Some story-related missions might give a different reputation and outcome based on your action, but you never have to worry about anything apart from that. I refrained from taking anything that might increase my black hat reputation at first, which only penalize me from getting a benefit from that category and more money.

Money is limited at the early game. This might give issues to those who are trying to play the game purely as white hats since they are restricted from taking money from certain nodes. Moreover, those who quit the mission halfway will get penalized even more since the mission will be treated as completed without getting any reward. The game will give you a lot of money near the end of the game, but you won't need it at that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759480074

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
The in-game clock says that I finished the game at 15:50:34, although [i]Steam[/i] said that I finished it in 26.6h. I had to retry some levels a few times to get a perfect result, and since you need to go to the main menu to buy more gears at the store in missions, it can take a while to load your save, especially with the unskippable animations. I spent the rest of my playtime figuring out the last achievement, which can be made shorter if you know what to do.

As for the difficulty, it can be hard at the beginning due to the RNG, but you can always change the difficulty in the options. I didn't change it apart from one mission, which I deemed impossible to finish at the normal difficulty due to the time limit. The final boss might also pose a problem if you choose to go on a certain route, although it is still doable by using certain programs.

[b]Problems[/b]
Some text can be hard to see due to the font color. Also, the in-game display can hinder you from seeing some information, such as the node address and how many turns you have left.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] might be unpleasant to play at first due to the RNG, but it will soon be enjoyable once you have access to certain upgrades. My focus went to completing missions instead of the story, which is always unique in certain aspects. The game also offers more gameplay through the Workshop feature, although I soon got bored since I had to deal with the RNG again without my upgrades. Although I found some aspects to be lacking, I still could recommend [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] at a sale, provided that you are fine with the RNG-based gameplay.

review_text_raw:
Context: I have finished the game. I did not 100% the game. But I find it hard to say how far I got from 100%ing the game, because I had no side content available to me at the time that I crossed the (helpfully labeled) point of no return, with the exception of the repeatable "virtual" addresses. But there are still definitely things that I let get away from me.

The very fact that I finished this game in two days with 18 hours logged should indicate a very strong positive review. But let me go into some details to make it more useful as well as providing some criticism.

Midnight Protocol is a hacking themed puzzle game with RPG elements and a strong central narrative. You play as a hacker who goes by Data on the net. You were doxxed and detained by the authorities before the game starts and went AWOL, but now you're back in the game, meet up with some old friends with your old terminal, and try to chase down the people who doxxed you. (This is the beginning of the story, you can pick this much up from just the demo). Without going any further (until later in the review), I will say the narrative is quite gripping. You definitely want to know what happens next.

Mechanically, you enter a network and move around between its various nodes doing various things. You encounter programs called ICE that try to impede your progress, and have your own programs for dispatching them. Slightly later in the game you encounter other users called SysOps who also interfere with you. These and just the general passage of time in the network all cause a trace counter to tick down. Once it hits zero, it stays that way, and in the next few turns you start to be directly affected: you start losing credits and soon you get a game over due to your location being exposed, unless you exit the network. You have various stealth tools that you can use to make this proceed slower, but for most of the game you still need to keep moving to avoid maxing out your trace. Some missions also have turn timers for objectives or even the whole mission, which further add to the pressure. 

Overall between the narrative and mechanics this game is extremely engrossing, even addicting. 

The aforementioned pressure ties into the first of my mechanical complaints about the game. That is that this game has a bit of an identity crisis in regards to permanence of your decisions and consequences. On the one hand, once you exit a mission, everything you did gets saved. Additionally, the game does not provide you with tools to facilitate chasing down multiple branches in decisions; in game there are only three save slots, even. So the game clearly wants you to play the game straight through at least the first time. On the other hand, while you are in a mission, you can roll it back to the start and even reconfigure your equipment. The actual network will be the same, although enemies that have their own turns may behave differently. (Edit: a patch after this review was originally written changed it so the network will not just be identical upon return.) This would be an accessibility feature that you could just ignore if you have more of a hardcore mentality, except that trying to play this game "blind and iron man mode" would be brutally difficult, so rolling back is sorta there to stay. 

The rollback also trivializes some of the levels that are based on reading off some information from the network to determine what to do and then doing that. For example there is a level where there are numerous nodes you can tamper with, and you need to interact with some other nodes to determine which one you actually need to tamper with. Once you have the intel, you almost might as well just roll back right there, because the node you need to tamper with is going to be the same after the reload anyway, and you are likely already getting pretty low on spare trace points.

My second mechanical complaint about the game is about one of the programs you get late in the game, and what it does to the flow of a lot of the lategame levels. Earlier in the game, you can't halt the passive trace entirely. The best you could do was slow it down by 75%, and even doing that greatly limits your options. This would tend to force you to either really optimize your methodology (usually requiring lots of rollbacks) or else sacrifice some possible gains (e.g. leaving money behind). But eventually you get a program that does halt it entirely, at the expense of some drawbacks that basically boil down to "take it slow". In some levels, this is perfectly well balanced because there is something else forcing a time pressure on you besides the passive trace. But in others, it just makes things feel plodding, as you slowly move around doing every last thing the network lets you do, with absolutely no risk of anything going awry. It starts feeling like the game is refusing to acknowledge that you've already solved the level.

My last mechanical complaint is a familiar one in a lot of games: there's a morality system, in the form of "white hat" reputation and "black hat" reputation. In-universe this makes perfect sense just like what these terms mean IRL. But it has a problem which is basically the opposite of the usual problem with morality systems, which is that there is not much "tug of war" going on. There is some, as some specific actions do get remembered in your save, but in general having both black rep and white rep is useful for unlocking new stuff to buy, so it doesn't really make sense to roleplay as a white hat or black hat hacker.

Speaking of roleplaying elements, my final complaint is about the narrative/character development, and there is absolutely no way to discuss this part in any detail without some pretty massive spoilers. [spoiler]Shortly before the point of no return, you view an autopsy report for the actual Data. The scene makes it sound like your character is as shocked to read this as you are as the player. But shortly after the point of no return, it is revealed that you were never Data. Instead you were working for a government digital security agency on a case that your employer thinks is related to Data. In general this twist is really powerful, except it has one extremely serious flaw: unlike you, your character knew almost all of this the entire time. So that part of the twist is sort of obtained by sleight of hand only, which makes it feel kinda cheap in hindsight. In particular it makes you wonder about the meaning of your loyalty to Data's close friends Clover and Snail. It also raises the question: who is even tracing you earlier in the game? You initially have the impression that it is the police, but if the police came to talk to you in person, presumably you could just flash your credentials and send them on their way. Who it actually is seems more fuzzy with that reveal in place. This also makes the meaning of a game over (at least before the point of no return) really unclear, because surely you would pull out some kind of secret trick that runs the risk of blowing your cover rather than being killed by corporate thugs or whatever.[/spoiler] The short and spoiler-free version of that wall of spoiler-tagged text is that there is a twist towards the end of the story that is somewhat unearned and sort of retroactively undermines some of the stuff that came before it.

I realize I just spent five paragraphs bashing this game, but it really has been one of the best games I've played in a long time. Only that last complaint actually feels like it isn't just the bad aspect of something that is both good and bad; all three of my mechanical complaints are deeply related to some of the things that make the mechanics really fun. And the story really is gripping, even with the defect I described in the spoiler. 

I highly recommend it. I especially would recommend it to fans of Cultist Simulator. The theme and mechanics are both very different but it somehow scratches some very similar itches nonetheless.

(Edit: a patch after this review was originally written changed it so the network will not just be identical upon return.) This would be an accessibility feature that you could just ignore if you have more of a hardcore mentality, except that trying to play this game "blind and iron man mode" would be brutally difficult, so rolling back is sorta there to stay. The rollback also trivializes some of the levels that are based on reading off some information from the network to determine what to do and then doing that. For example there is a level where there are numerous nodes you can tamper with, and you need to interact with some other nodes to determine which one you actually need to tamper with. Once you have the intel, you almost might as well just roll back right there, because the node you need to tamper with is going to be the same after the reload anyway, and you are likely already getting pretty low on spare trace points. My second mechanical complaint about the game is about one of the programs you get late in the game, and what it does to the flow of a lot of the lategame levels. Earlier in the game, you can't halt the passive trace entirely. The best you could do was slow it down by 75%, and even doing that greatly limits your options. This would tend to force you to either really optimize your methodology (usually requiring lots of rollbacks) or else sacrifice some possible gains (e.g. leaving money behind). But eventually you get a program that does halt it entirely, at the expense of some drawbacks that basically boil down to "take it slow". In some levels, this is perfectly well balanced because there is something else forcing a time pressure on you besides the passive trace. But in others, it just makes things feel plodding, as you slowly move around doing every last thing the network lets you do, with absolutely no risk of anything going awry. It starts feeling like the game is refusing to acknowledge that you've already solved the level. My last mechanical complaint is a familiar one in a lot of games: there's a morality system, in the form of "white hat" reputation and "black hat" reputation. In-universe this makes perfect sense just like what these terms mean IRL. But it has a problem which is basically the opposite of the usual problem with morality systems, which is that there is not much "tug of war" going on. There is some, as some specific actions do get remembered in your save, but in general having both black rep and white rep is useful for unlocking new stuff to buy, so it doesn't really make sense to roleplay as a white hat or black hat hacker. Speaking of roleplaying elements, my final complaint is about the narrative/character development, and there is absolutely no way to discuss this part in any detail without some pretty massive spoilers. [spoiler]Shortly before the point of no return, you view an autopsy report for the actual Data. The scene makes it sound like your character is as shocked to read this as you are as the player. But shortly after the point of no return, it is revealed that you were never Data. Instead you were working for a government digital security agency on a case that your employer thinks is related to Data. In general this twist is really powerful, except it has one extremely serious flaw: unlike you, your character knew almost all of this the entire time. So that part of the twist is sort of obtained by sleight of hand only, which makes it feel kinda cheap in hindsight. In particular it makes you wonder about the meaning of your loyalty to Data's close friends Clover and Snail. It also raises the question: who is even tracing you earlier in the game? You initially have the impression that it is the police, but if the police came to talk to you in person, presumably you could just flash your credentials and send them on their way. Who it actually is seems more fuzzy with that reveal in place. This also makes the meaning of a game over (at least before the point of no return) really unclear, because surely you would pull out some kind of secret trick that runs the risk of blowing your cover rather than being killed by corporate thugs or whatever.[/spoiler] The short and spoiler-free version of that wall of spoiler-tagged text is that there is a twist towards the end of the story that is somewhat unearned and sort of retroactively undermines some of the stuff that came before it. I realize I just spent five paragraphs bashing this game, but it really has been one of the best games I've played in a long time. Only that last complaint actually feels like it isn't just the bad aspect of something that is both good and bad; all three of my mechanical complaints are deeply related to some of the things that make the mechanics really fun. And the story really is gripping, even with the defect I described in the spoiler. I highly recommend it. I especially would recommend it to fans of Cultist Simulator. The theme and mechanics are both very different but it somehow scratches some very similar itches nonetheless.

review_text_raw:
An enjoyable investigative puzzle game, Midnight Protocol has good writing, reinforced by clever changes in the UI and the visual respresentation of dataspace with every level. The game succeeds in creating the appropriate mood when it needs to, with music that alters alongside the tension, or meta elements involving a desktop crash or UI corruption. Some of the puzzles require innovative thinking, or a re-examination of what is at your disposal, which makes it rewarding to find a solution.

The strategic part comes through the deck and hardware customisation, which is well-tied into the story and gameplay. Optional challenges for extra credits encourage change; combined with mission-required programs and the natural slot limit, it encourages you to think and change your plan as required. I found the 'rollback' command, allowing the player to retry the mission with a different loadout, to be an essential part of adapting an approach, as the tactics to complete an actual level is tied heavily into your loadout choices. No prior knowledge of programming is required to play, and the game provides in-level help for any command the player needs.

The percentage chance for trace progression, which leads to a level's failure condition, is something that might appear frustrating if the player has few options (such as near the beginning of the game with limited programs available), but no level is impossible, and as a turn-based game with unlimited retries, there is plenty of time to think and plan, which makes the eventual success more satisfying.

At face value I was uncertain, but after twenty-eight hours of playtime and playing nothing else until I finished it, I am certain that Midnight Protocol is a good game that could be worth your attention.

I don't write reviews very often but this game deserves one.   Midnight Protocol is an accessible hacker game where it really makes you feel like you are hacking without having to have all the technical know-how.    You input commands into a terminal (via keyboard, how novel!) but there are not so many as to feel overwhelming.  In fact a few basic commands are designed to make it as transparent as possible (such as 'deck' which will remind you what you have equipped).  Some programs also have options and a simple 'help' command will remind you how to input them.  The game really hits the sweetspot with accessibility and it also has nice ambiance and interesting story line.    

I enjoyed the variety of programs and deck hardware to choose from though i found some quite powerful, some quite situational, and some unnecessary but there is a lot of fun in figuring that out for yourself.   While early on i used the standard 'cloak' and 'dagger' everyone starts with, i evolved my strategy to use 'mask' which is powerful but slow but wound up enjoying using 'onion' the most.   Combine that with the hardware that gives a modest stealth boost and see what happens!   Takes some discipline though.

I also randomly and luckily equipped 'Ace' and 'King' in the hack where it is needed the most.  It made the hack a breeze but I couldn't think of needing these programs in any other hack.  As I said, quite situational.  But the game is quite forgiving and as long as you have a program or piece of hardware in your inventory, you can easily rollback the hack and re-equip what you need to start that hack over.  
The rollback feature may make the game even a little too easy but with that said, i found the game engaging and rare for me, something i concentrated on completing before i got distracted by my next game!   My main criticism of the game may be that, while i don't want to go into detail and spoil it, there were components of the plot i didn't like.  Let's just say it was controversial.   But overall the meaningful side quests and decisions that you make but come back to help or haunt you help make the overall experience quite fun.

I would highly recommend this to anyone interested in the hacking universe and good story telling (all revealed via email).  As I write this i even have to remember i have a mouse I can use and don't have to only use the keyboard!  Enjoy!

Super cool and slick hacker game inspired by Netrunner. The greatest CCG ever produced. 


The early game was rough though until I got Mask finally after completing Act 1. (So I was slicing Cloak a lot and getting wrecked by trace)

The story goes places for sure. Huge twist near the end of the game. The last push is a bit longer than I expected and some of the best missions are kind of hidden including one banger involving Hacker Chess in your desktop Apps. Even though I got these secret missions I still royally botched a few quest lines that went unresolved. () I think you can easily close off the end of a quest line if you respond to an email incorrectly. Not ideal. Otherwise I completed everything I could.

Beyond is just musings about mechanics, beware:

I used “most” of the programs but some I couldn’t figure out how they worked or they were super niche. I basically alternated between a “gotta go fast” Tunnel build and a slow stealth build using Mask, which does synergize well with Hive. Buzzkiller was my blunt breaker of choice that replaced Dagger until Vorpalsword or Shuriken (ultra late game). Leech and Spoon remained useful throughout the entire game as does Trolltoll. I tried but couldn’t make King and Ace work at all. The upgrades to some programs felt like downgrades instead (namely Cloak and Sniffer). Sniper is situationally useful on some missions. Barrier with sysops but I only ended up needing it a couple times. Buffer against trace and Overclock for extra movement naturally. That’s about it. One thing that was super apparent though after loading into dozens of missions is…oh gosh I definitely need this, this, and this…time to rollback. (And the white on white menu is terrible here)

P.S. I ended up maxing White Hat and Grey Hat but not Black Hat so I never saw their late game programs so I can’t speak to those. Apparently the game’s story changes a bit if you do max Black Hat instead.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is an excellent dive into 'HACKER CULTURE' a la Cyberpunk. Playing in a future universe, you manipulate an archaic-feeling digital terminal to hack into networks, remove defenses, and save the world from corpo scum. The mechanics are simple - almost exclusively text based - and feel immersive. I felt smug dodging enemy admins, clever when I guessed passwords based on information I'd gathered, and accomplished when I completed missions that had been giving me trouble. It delivers on its promises.

The plot was unexpectedly good, far exceeding my expectations. I understand there are multiple endings as well, though I only played through the once. I enjoyed it a lot. I will say no more for spoiler reasons.

My only critique is that the game feels like a puzzle game, but frequently makes it very difficult to solve the puzzle without resetting the level. While I don't mind it, many might feel like this is 'save scumming' and I wish there was a better way to resolve not having the right programs to handle a challenge than just resetting. They do minimize you ability to 'cheat' my randomizing many defenses between attempts, but the information gain is still significant at times.

Overall, I would strongly recommend this game. I finished it with 52 hours on the Steam clock, but I believe I left it on overnight. I managed to beat it in a couple of days of dedicated play. For the price, it was a great time!
